Mr. Bourgon

For this reason, if the Trial Chamber agrees, we could close our case today and reserve the right to submit those arguments or rather the extra information indicated in this list at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we have to turn to Mr. Mundis here. utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, in principle, we have no objection; of course, we would need to see the documents prior to having any final position with respect to the documents, but as of this point in time, we certainly have no objection to this type of procedure being followed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right, then. We have taken note of that. The Prosecution will of course study the document that you've drafted today and then we shall talk about it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. So you said a fortnight, but the last document will be translated when? If it's within this week, it's okay, but if it's in a month, it is going to be a month plus two weeks. So as of when?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Thank you. Would that date, the 15th of May be convenient to the Prosecution in order for you to study all these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, he we would not anticipate any problem with meeting that deadline if our learned colleagues could perhaps indicate either on the record or by a written notification that all of the materials have in fact been translated and we of course receive copies of all of that material, we will endeavour to review it as quickly as possible. I certainly don't think there will be any problem with a deadline of 15 May, assuming that we have them by the third week or the end of the third week of April. That certainly wouldn't be a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well then. Mr. Bourgon, the Prosecution wishes to receive the documents as soon as possible and then, of course, the 15th of May is the deadline for their point of view. So as of the 15th of May, we will give our opinion or, rather, our approval if there are no other problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, we fully agree with the Prosecution. As soon as the last one of the 81 missing documents in terms of translations is submitted, we shall immediately notify them officially in order to confirm that the dossier has been completed. Mr. President, you have to take account of the fact that all the documents that have been submitted today together with our final list are already available to the Prosecution. What's currently missing are the 81 translations which are still missing. But as to everything else, they already have all the documents available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Except that the Trial Chamber doesn't have all those documents but we'll have them soon. So the Trial Chamber accepts -- takes note of the fact that they can close the case today but of course with the proviso that we still get those documents according to the modalities that we have heard about over the past few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours, for the sake of the transcript, I would just like to say that with regard to the Defence of General Hadzihasanovic, I would just like to state once again formally that we have closed our case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now we shall move on to the next stage and it was my understanding that there would be an opening statement now. So we are in open session, so in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. There will be an opening statement now on behalf of Mr. Kubura, and he will also use this opportunity to address Your Honours pursuant to Rule 84 bis after I've completed my opening statement. It will last just over an hour and I would propose that I commence now and find an appropriate place to break for the technical break and then continue thereafter to be followed then by Mr. Kubura's short statement to Your Honours. As Your Honours will be aware, it is always said of lengthy criminal trials like the one that we have been involved in for some 206 days now, that no matter how complex the case might first appear, the path to discovering the truth is invariably one which depends on a very small number of crucial and narrow factual questions, Your Honours. Questions which we say that mostly always have simple answers and complicated answers, once all the irrelevant material has been stripped away. Mr. Kubura's Defence is very clear and to the point. This is how it happened, we say. For the killings in Miletici and Maline, as they are alleged in the indictment, no members or units of the 7th Brigade were there at the relevant time - that being 24th April and 6 June 1993, respectively; I apologise, 8 June, 1993 - let alone involved in the commission of any crimes on these days. For the music school and Motel Sretno, in our submission, there's not a shred of evidence that Mr. Kubura knew or had reason to know about any particular beatings that occurred at these places. On the contrary, there are reasons why he would not have had information at his disposal. For the alleged destruction and looting in the Ovnak area and Vares, in some instances, there is simply no evidence presented by the Prosecution of destruction. And in others, no evidence of the identity of the perpetrators. In circumstances where various brigades and units were involved in the military operations, civilians were on the loose, and many of the alleged crimes were committed when units of the 7th Brigade were no longer even present in the area. Finally, throughout all of these alleged incidents, Mr. Kubura was only appointed as the commander of the 7th Brigade from the 6th August 1993. A simple defence, Your Honours, but not a simplistic one. There is a big difference, in our submission. When the historical expert, Professor Cihic [phoen] was asked by the Prosecution in cross-examination, and I quote here, it was Ms. Henry-Benjamin who asked the question. These were her words, "So then would I be correct in assuming or saying that the 7th Brigade accommodated the Muslim race so that your foreigners, who might have been Muslims, they automatically would have gone to the 7th Brigade; am I correct?" His answer was, "I think that would be a simplistic interpretation." In our view, simplistic here, Your Honours, means naive, one dimensional, and in our submission that is an apt description of the whole of the Prosecution's case against our client. I say this with the greatest respect to my colleagues from the Office of the Prosecutor who we have worked with and cooperated with the best and most professional of spirits throughout this case. But they have simply got it wrong. Their case oversimplifies matters and relies on sweeping generalisations without any hard evidence to back-up those assertions. There are too many leaps too far, in our submission. To illustrate my point, Your Honours, at the heart of this case, and for which it will always be remembered in the records of international criminal law, is the presence of foreign fighters, Mujahedin. Who is criminally responsible for their actions is an ultimate issue in this case. A simplistic proposition by the Prosecution by way of example has been that MOS, the Muslim forces that which you have heard about, was formed in 1992 and it included foreigners who had arrived in Central Bosnia. The Prosecution then go on to say that the MOS became the 7th Brigade wholesale. They said this in their 98 bis submission and Mr. Mundis said this in oral argument, and I quote his words directly; he said, "Our case has been one, and we explained this in our 98 bis submission, that the Travnik Muslim forces evolved into the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade." He said that on the 24th of October, 2004. And the Prosecution then go on to say Mr. Kubura must have effectively controlled foreign fighters including those who allegedly committed the offences in late April and early June 1993. But they don't finish there. They take it further to say, well suddenly in August, 1993, the Mujahedin were moved, the Prosecution say, into a new unit called the El Mujahed Unit. Now, in our submission, Your Honours, such a theory is both riddled with assertions that have absolutely no factual basis on the evidence we have heard. For instance, there is no evidence that all or any foreigners were incorporated into the MOS. There's no evidence that the MOS was transformed into the 7th Brigade. As an aside, Mr. Kubura was never even a member of the MOS. And there's also no evidence that later any foreigners were moved from the 7th Brigade into the El Mujahed unit. This theory, in our view, is riddled with leaps of logic that can never be used to prove criminal responsibility beyond reasonable doubt. For instance, why would there be any need to form an El Mujahed unit to accommodate foreigners if they were already in the army and neatly all under the control of the 7th Brigade of the 3rd Corps? Has the Prosecution come up with an answer to that question? No, we say. But what is the Prosecution's case? It has never been clear from day one until today or ever been stated in our view with any certainty or confidence by the Prosecution. They have a fundamental problem at the core of their case against Mr. Kubura. We say they cannot establish any connection between the 7th Brigade and the Mujahedin for the offences in Miletici and Maline. The Prosecution has tried four times to clarify the issue and come up with no less than four different stories and I'll go through each of those for Your Honours. The first started way back in July 2001, the original indictment Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. where, in paragraph 62, the Prosecution said that and I quote from the indictment, "With the creation of the ABiH 3rd Corps area of command, the Mujahedin were attached to and subordinated to the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. Subsequently, the Mujahedin were heavily involved in combat activities with the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. As principally an offensive unit, the Mujahedin frequently spearheaded operations." That means in our view, all Mujahedin, the Prosecution were saying, were actually in the 7th Brigade. In the rest of the indictment, they said that the 306th Brigade and the 7th Brigade attacked Miletici and Maline after which the crimes were committed. We then move on to January 2002, the second indictment. This indictment was an amendment of the first because we, as the Defence, had challenged the form of the indictment. We'd argued that it was imprecise, that the identity of the perpetrators was not clear, and who they were subordinated, which particular brigades, if any, was not made clear. What the Prosecution then did in response, paragraph 25 of the second indictment was they included the word "predominantly." They said that the Mujahedin were predominantly incorporated into the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. We then come to the third indictment which was the indictment before Your Honours for the trial, and we see two things. Firstly, the word "predominantly" is now removed. And secondly, the "the" which I referred to earlier on, "the Mujahedin" is also removed. So in paragraph 19, all it says now is that Mujahedin were incorporated and subordinated in the 7th Brigade. There is no indication which, whether it is some or all. The Prosecution has kept it vague, deliberately, we say, because they don't know what their case is. Also in the rest of the indictment, they continued with the allegation that the 306th and the 7th Brigade attacked Miletici and Maline after which the crimes were committed. That's paragraph 39. The fourth version, Your Honours, came out with the indictment of Mr. Rasim Delic, the indictment of 15 February, 2005. In paragraph 13 of that indictment, the Prosecution now allege the following: "That after its formation on 19 November 1992, the 7th Brigade incorporated Mujahedin into its structure as did other units of the ABiH 3rd Corps and the paragraph continues, "the Mujahedin were involved in combat activities of units of the ABiH 3rd Corps including the 7th Brigade and frequently spearheaded April 3rd corps combat operations." There are two points that arise. Here we see for the first time the OTP has alleged that the Mujahedin were in other units and involved in combat activities of units of the 3rd corps. Secondly, they now allege that Mujahedin spearheaded operations not of the 7th Brigade any longer, as they had said in all the other indictments, but just generally of the 3rd Corps. Moving on then to the alleged killings in Miletici and Maline. Paragraphs 25 and 25 of the Delic indictment are relevant, and I have a copy of that indictment here, Your Honours. And I would ask that it be put on the ELMO at those paragraphs, 24 and 25, so one can appreciate the changes that have been made. Starting with paragraph 24, which is just on the previous page, this regards the alleged killings in Maline. I will read the paragraph, Your Honours. "On 8 June 1993, the day that Rasim Delic assumed the post of commander of the Main Staff units of the ABiH 3rd Corps, including the 306th Mountain Brigade, the 7th Muslim Brigade, and the Mujahedin, launched an attack on the village of Maline in Travnik municipality." Pausing there, we see here for the first time the Prosecution now alleging that not only was it the 306th and the 7th but also the Mujahedin listed as a separate entity in the indictment. "Following the HVO surrender, more than 200 Bosnian Croat civilians and HVO soldiers were captured and ordered by the military police of the ABiH 306th Mountain Brigade to march towards Mehurici, a village several kilometres from Maline. As the this column was approaching the village of Poljanice, several hundred meters from Mehurici, a group of approximately ten Mujahedin and local Bosnian Muslim soldiers approached from the direction of Mehurici and ordered the column to stop." Pausing there, Your Honours, it is significant, we say, that there is no allegation that the 7th Brigade were involved at all with these prisoners and their escort or their kidnapping. It simply mentioned 10 Mujahedin and local Bosnian Muslim soldiers. We may ask: Is this change a result of the evidence that has been presented before Your Honours in this trial? Continuing then over the page to paragraph 25, "Shortly thereafter, this group met a smaller group of persons who had also been captured in Maline and the two groups proceeded towards Maline. When the group arrived at the junction that led to Bikosi, they were ordered to turn towards that village and, after arriving there, they were ordered to form a line. The Mujahedin then indiscriminately opened gunfire on the group, executing some of the survivors of this initial shooting by single gunshots to the head." We say, once again, it's significant that it's alleged by the Prosecution now that Mujahedin, not any brigades of the Bosnian army, not the 7th Brigade, committed these killings. It's still not alleged which particular Mujahedin, but the group of Mujahedin is referred to as "the perpetrators." Is this the result of evidence that has been presented before Your Honours in this case? In essence, we say that the OTP have conceded that the perpetrators were not in the 7th Brigade. They have accepted in the Delic indictment the case of the Defence. Thank you, Your Honours. I will not refer any longer to the indictment; it can be taken from the ELMO. Your Honours, before I turn to the counts in the indictment, a word about Mr. Kubura himself and his position in 1993. As the evidence will show, the narrative Amir Kubura's life at the time war broke out in Bosnia reads like that of so many ordinary persons and soldiers who were caught up in the painful events that were to follow. Mr. Kubura will tell Your Honours more about his background when he makes his statement. But in summary, he was with his wife and children in Kosovo at the beginning of 1992. He was stationed there in a time of peace as an officer of the JNA. A young man of 29 years old with a young family, unaware of how dramatically their lives were about to change. His late mother and other family members were living in the town of Kakanj in Bosnia; that's the town of his birth. He had grown up there, gone to school there before joining the JNA to undertake his military training. As we all began to learn with great trepidation from the media and on our television sets, in early 1992 the war was spreading from Slovenia and Croatia into neighbouring Bosnia and Herzegovina. The horrifying spectre of ethnic cleansing arose for the first time, a new term that had been fashioned to describe the treatment meted out on innocent civilians by advancing Serb forces and paramilitary groupings. When Mr. Kubura heard that fighting was breaking out all over Bosnia and that his home region was now also under threat, he took the hard decision to return to Kakanj in Bosnia to be there for his family, to defend his country. It was a defining moment for him. He was out of Bosnia at the time. He could have left the region like so many other people did but he wanted to be there to return, to serve, to help, to do what he could do. That was the overriding impulse that drove him. He was not a political man; the evidence will show this. Not a member of any political party. Not an outspoken religious person. He had never been in any trouble before and had never stood out for any reason, good or bad. He had an uncontroversial background and a reasonably promising career that was on track. He was a young, typical JNA officer, one of many who had never fought in armed conflict, although trained to, but never believed that he would. As a person, he was well liked and popular. People at work and in his social life warmed to him easily. He had that rare quality to be respected by both friends and foe alike. Your Honours, at his core, a good man. I'll say no more about this, Your Honours; the evidence about him will emerge. But to pause there for a moment and ask a question: Is this why the Mujahedin sought to assassinate him in the summer of 1993? Something we have heard about from the international witnesses and something that is recorded in their reports. He represented everything that they sought to destroy. They were waging, as the indictment alleges, a holy war, and people like the I ill-fated victims of the Mujahedin and like Mr. Kubura could be expended in the name of that cause. It would be a mockery, we say, to suggest that he commanded these people or could have punished them. Mr. Kubura could not be apart from his family, and they accompanied him to Kakanj, arriving there in May of 1992, and he immediately joined the TO in Kakanj. On 5 September 1992, he was appointed of the deputy commander of the 1st Battalion of the armed forces of Kakanj municipality and was appointed as the commander of this Battalion on 1 December 1992. As Your Honours have heard in the evidence, towards the end of the 1992, the corps and the brigades in the Bosnian army were beginning to be established, one such brigade being the 7th Brigade which Your Honours have heard much about already in this trial. It was formed as part of the 3rd Corps by the Supreme Command Staff order dated 19 November 1993. Mr. Kubura was not involved at all in the formation of this brigade. As I've mentioned already, he was a member of the armed forces of the Kakanj municipality at the time. He was assigned to the 7th Brigade by order on 11 December 1992 to the position of assistant chief of staff for operational and educational affairs. These allegations regarding his background are set out in paragraph 6 of the indictment, Your Honours. There are some inaccuracies, we say, in those allegations which should be corrected at the outset. The first is that by a Supreme Command Staff order, Mr. Kubura was appointed as chief of staff and deputy commander of the 7th Brigade on 12 March 1993 and not 1 January 1993 as is stated in the indictment. Your Honours have seen this document when the military expert testified and it will be introduced as evidence during our Defence case. Mr. Koricic was appointed as the brigade commander at the same time. Thereafter, by a Supreme Command staff order dated 6 August 1993, Mr. Kubura was appointed as the commander of the 7th Brigade. He did not become the commander on 21 July 1993 as is stated in the indictment. DK25 is the document regarding his appointment on 6 August 1993. Before this date, we say it is for the Prosecution to prove what his position was and over whom he exercised effective control, if any. The indictment alleges from 1 April 1993 he acted as the substitute for Mr. Koricic, and the indictment continues "the then-assigned 7th Brigade commander who was absent during this period." Where is the evidence to support this allegation that Mr. Koricic was absent and that Mr. Kubura became his substitute? Mr. Mundis said, when cross-examining the expert, that it was a gap in the expert's report that he could not conclude where Mr. Koricic was and whether he was still the commander. We say this is a gap in the Prosecution's case. The Prosecution try to fill this gap by saying Mr. Koricic went to recruit Mujahedins in Croatia. On the 14th of December last year, Mr. Mundis said, and I quote his words, "I suggest to you that Mr. Asim Koricic left Central Bosnia on 31 March 1993 and that he went to Croatia and was involved in importing foreigners into Central Bosnia and that he did so on behalf of the 3rd Corps." There is not an ounce of evidence to support this sweeping allegation. Another example, we say, of a leap too far. Rather, the evidence is, and there are four points that I wish to summarise here, firstly, that Mr. Kubura was not the formally appointed commander until 6 August. There's no official appointment to acting commander or any other position as there ought to have been according to the military regulations. That's Article 78 which was referred to the military expert. No one was appointed as chief of staff to replace Mr. Kubura. Secondly, the documents from the 7th Brigade in this case before August 1993 that are signed by the commander were done in the name of Asim Koricic as the commander, even documents in June and July 1993. Some were signed by Mr. Kubura but some were signed by other persons. Your Honours will recall the testimony of the military expert: A commander is a commander wherever he might be. Thirdly, Mr. Kubura was not the prominent face of the 7th Brigade. Your Honours will recall that almost all the international witnesses had never heard about him, never met him, never had any reason to seek him out. The 7th Brigade member who testified, Witness BA, even said he thought Mr. Kubura was in Germany at the time. You will recall he was one of the early witnesses called by the Prosecution. Fourthly, Your Honours will also recall what even Mr. Totic, who could be regarded as Mr. Kubura's main adversary stated in his testimony, he said, "There were other more influential people in the brigade." That was on the 23rd of February, 2004. Now, Your Honours, Mr. Kubura is not suggesting for a moment that he did not person form functions in the 7th Brigade or, for that matter, that he was in Germany at the time. That's not his defence. He's never challenged his position in the brigade. But Your Honours must consider, on the evidence presented, what his concrete position as a young officer was before August 1993. Your Honours must assess what powers, in fact, he possessed and what information in his position he may in reality have been exposed to. And this should be done against the backdrop, Your Honours, of the well-settled law on the responsibilities of staff officers which was set out in the High Command case, the case tried by the United States military tribunal after the Second World War. I quote a small section from that case which was referred to in the Celebici judgement at paragraph 367. It reads, "Staff officers are indispensable in the link" -- I will start again, Your Honours. "Staff officers are an indispensable link in the chain of the execution of orders. Since a chief of staff does not have command authority in the chain of command, an order over his signature does not have authority for subordinates in the chain of command. A failure to properly exercise command responsibility is not the responsibility of a chief of staff. In the absence of participation in criminal orders, or the execution within a command, a chief of staff does not become criminally responsible for criminal acts occurring therein. He has no command authority over subordinate's units. All he can do in such cases is call those matters to the attention of his commanding General. Command authority and responsibility forwards exercise rest definitively upon his commander." Your Honours, in the indictment at paragraphs 36 to 38, the Prosecution set out what they allege Mr. Kubura's powers were. And in a nutshell, they say at all relevant times by virtue of his position and authority, he commanded all units of the 7th Brigade including those operating detention facilities. The question must be asked, we say: Has the Prosecution proved those allegations and that Mr. Kubura acted as the commander or acting commander from 1 April 1993? Where is the evidence that he had de facto control of all commanding officers and troops of the 7th Brigade? It is correct, as the Prosecution say that in military terms, someone is always in command. But the question is who and with what powers? What is clear from the evidence is that the 7th Brigade was a manoeuvre unit, one of many in the 3rd Corps which is not unusual. Without a fixed area of responsibility, it was not fully replenished. Your Honours will recall the report of August 1993 where its manpower levels were listed at 76 per cent. The total numbers of the brigade were roughly 1.400 troops with its members assigned, like all other brigades, by the municipal defence staff. People drawn from the surrounding villages, ordinary people, joining up to defend their towns and their villages together with refugees. Looking further about other allegations that are made about the brigade in the indictment, paragraph 17, Your Honours. There is, in our submission, and this will be borne out by the witnesses who are called in our case, that there is no evidence that this unit was required to strictly adhere to Islamic beliefs. No evidence that recruits had to swear an oath to follow the example of a proper Muslim soldier, as is set out in the instructions to the Muslim fighter. And no evidence that 20.000 copies of this were distributed in the 3rd Corps area of responsibility. Once again, leaps too far, we say, by the Prosecution. Mr. Kubura was based at the headquarters of the 7th Brigade as its chief of staff but he operated in the field and on the front lines coordinating particular military operations. Your Honours will hear evidence about this. His main operations were in Ovnak in May and June of 1993 and Vares in October and November 1993, as is evidenced by the documents in this trial. For example, DK23 and 24, they are the plans and orders relating to the operations of the 7th Brigade immediately after the operation in Ovnak. They were both signed by Mr. Kubura as chief of staff on 10 and 11 June respectively. It is significant that there are no similar documents for any operations in Maline and Miletici because the 7th Brigade was not there. As an aside, Your Honours, I do wish to add that there are other documents where Mr. Kubura signed as chief of staff during this time, not as anything else. On the context of these operations, and I will finish with this point before continuing after the break, we will not lead evidence about the context of the operations that occurred. But there is one point which must be made at this stage. It is important to keep some perspective. The broad context of these alleged offences, which is not set out in the indictment, is in our submission, the ethnic cleansing campaigns conducted by the Bosnian Serb forces under the direction of Belgrade and the HVO with the support from Croatia against the largely Muslim population of Bosnia. The aim was to gain control of parts of Bosnia and create greater Serbias and greater Croatias respectively. This conclusion has been confirmed in various judgements of the ICTY, including the Kordic judgement, which was not overturned on appeal. And there, the Trial Chamber said that there was overwhelming evidence of a campaign of persecution in 1992 and 1993 aimed at the Bosnian Muslim population. The most important part which I wish to emphasise is that the Trial Chamber held that the Defence case, that's the Defence of Mr. Kordic, "that these events amounted to a civil war in which the Bosnian Croats were on the defensive and themselves subject to persecution is rejected." That's at paragraph 827 of the Kordic judgement. The Prosecution cannot have it both ways. They can't say in Kordic that the HVO were on the offensive, which was accepted by the Trial Chamber, but then suddenly in our case they are on the defensive. Of course, Your Honours, a war crime is a war crime. It's not a defence to say the other side was attacking and committing worse crimes. But we can also not pretend that this trial is divorced from the position that the OTP has taken in other cases. Over and over again, and it's been accepted by the Trial Chambers, the OTP has stated that the conflicts in Bosnia were driven by the raw political and territorial ambitions of the then-leadership of Serbia and Croatia. I will return now to my opening point which is the key factual issues that this case turns on. Perhaps after the break, Your Honours, I can move to those very specific issues. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dixon, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. In the case of Mr. Kubura, we say the ultimate issue is: Were any of the perpetrators, Mujahedin or otherwise, of the alleged killings in Miletici and Maline under the effective control of Mr. Kubura in the sense that they were his subordinates with him able to prevent or punish their actions. That is the key question. Your Honours have heard all of the evidence, the answer must be "no." No, because the 7th Brigade was not deployed or present at these places, and no, because the Mujahedin or their followers who were present in Mehurici, which I referred to as the nerve centre of the alleged offences, where they were perpetrated from, none of those persons were in any way linked to the 7th Brigade and for the purposes of Article 7(3) under the effective control of Mr. Kubura. As we have said all along, there are only three ways that the Prosecution can prove Mr. Kubura is liable. Either they have to show that members of the 7th Brigade were present and involved in the commission of those offences on those days. The answer to that is that there's absolutely no evidence of presence and perpetration of the offences. So they must move on to the second leg, which is they can try and prove that all the Mujahedin were under the effective control of Mr. Kubura including those stationed in the camp in Mehurici. The answer to that, Your Honours, is that on their own case, I cited the Delic case earlier on, they can't prove that all Mujahedin were incorporated in the 7th Brigade. So they have to move on to the third option which is that they have to show who were the particular individual Mujahedin or people who committed the offences and then show that those people were under the effective control of Mr. Kubura. We say that option can be crossed out as well because the Prosecution have conceded that they cannot identify who the precise perpetrators of the offences were. They said as much in their 98 bis submission. They said, "We cannot identify the individual perpetrators with any degree of specificity." And they haven't led any evidence to show who the particular individuals were. But let's take it step by step, Your Honours. Part A will be: The 7th Brigade was not present. And here, I wish to briefly summarise the main Defence points as they will be confirmed by the evidence in the case for Mr. Kubura. Firstly, as we've said on many occasions, the Prosecution's own expert, General Reinhardt, confirmed, having looked at all the evidence in the case, there was no evidence of a presence of a 7th Brigade. That was confirmed by the Defence military expert as well. Secondly, the oral evidence confirms exactly the same. Witness after witness has stated that the 7th Brigade, and in particular they were looking at the 1st Battalion stationed in the town of Travnik, was not in Miletici and Maline. Your Honours have heard from the commander of the 306th Brigade, Mr. Sipic, and the testimony of no less than 16 witnesses from the 306th Brigade, all confirming that the 7th Brigade was not there and involved. If the 1st Battalion was in Mehurici, in our submission there would be no reason for the local commanders like Mr. Sipic to seek to protect the 7th Brigade. Quite the contrary, in fact. There are no allegations in any of the 306 documents, in any of the command documents from the 3rd Corps or any of the supreme command documents that the 7th Brigade was involved or responsible in any way. Thirdly, witnesses have confirmed that the 1st Battalion was elsewhere on the relevant dates. And during the case for Mr. Kubura, we will call witnesses from the 1st Battalion who will state exactly where they were and what they were doing on those days. Fourthly, as Your Honours will be aware, there is a host of documentation regarding the activities of the forces on that day. Many of them have been shown during the Defence case for Mr. Hadzihasanovic. Your Honours will recall the document from General Alagic of 8 June 1993, that's P465, clearly showing that the 7th Brigade was not in Maline on that day. Your Honours will also recall the war diaries of the 306th Brigade and the OG Bosanska Krajina documents which were not introduced by the Prosecution for the relevant days. And they match up, they both confirm the 7th Brigade was not involved, and they outline which brigades and units were involved. There are many similar documents which will be shown to our witnesses and they will explain the activities of the 7th Brigade on those days. Fifthly, the lack of presence of the 7th Brigade is confirmed by the reporting about what happened for the incidents in Miletici and Maline. Your Honours will recall complaints being made, inquiries being made, and then letters being sent from people like Mr. Delalic, Mr. Dugalic, and ultimately Mr. Merdan in November 1993. None of those documents mention involvement of the 7th Brigade. All inquiries about what happened were either sent to the OG or to the 306th Brigade. Nothing was ever sent to the 7th Brigade about these incidents. And the 7th Brigade was not involved at all in the investigations that properly followed those incidents. Part B, Your Honour, is that there is no link with the Mujahedin in respect of Miletici and Maline. In the Prosecution's 98 bis submission, they alleged that the Mujahedin were deployed including with the 7th Brigade. But we say if there is no evidence that the 7th Brigade was present, it is impossible for the foreigners to have been deployed with them, as the Prosecution say. The Prosecution case must become, and of course it's for them to say this, but it must become, although it might seem odd, that the Mujahedin in Mehurici were under the effective control of Mr. Kubura even if no 7th Brigade command or members were present there. But we return to the original question: Who were the perpetrators? If they cannot be identified, how can the Prosecution even begin to try and prove their case, begin to try and prove who was effectively controlled by Mr. Kubura? Your Honours, there are admitted documents, the majority of which were admitted without any witness, purportedly from the 7th Brigade which mentioned foreigners. Taken at their very highest, the Prosecution could argue that they indicate an association with some foreigners. But they can't argue with all foreigners, and they cannot use any of those documents to argue a link with the foreigners, particularly those in the camp at Mehurici, and then the particular perpetrators. We say that only documents concerning the foreigners in Mehurici or those connected with the offences in Miletici and Maline are relevant in respect of the ultimate issue which I outlined earlier for Mr. Kubura. In the event, no witnesses have been called by the OTP on these documents, even though we have contested them. They had been admitted, but as Your Honours have stated, weight has not been determined as yet. The Prosecution cannot expect Mr. Kubura to fill in the gaps during his case. We are not obliged to call witnesses in our case to address documents which have nothing to do with Miletici and Maline. The OTP could have called the authors of these documents if they had wanted to. Moreover, the documents in this case do not, as the Prosecution have said on many occasions, speak for themselves. The documents merely confirm words on a page but not the truth of their contents. It's only witnesses that can bring these documents to life and permit Your Honours to assess the probative value. Otherwise, anybody could write a document claiming that they are innocent and submit it for the truth of its contents and say, "Well, the document speaks for itself." In summary, Your Honours, the Prosecution's evidence simply does not prove that the Mujahedin perpetrators were with the 7th Brigade and under the effective control of Mr. Kubura. Not a single witness has said that and not a single document states that. On the contrary, the Prosecution's own military expert, General Reinhardt, stated, and I must stress here, this is not the case of the Defence, but it's what the Prosecution has stated in its case. He said, "You could not say who from the foreigners may be in the brigade or out of the brigade." His words were, "It was dubious to me." So on the Prosecution's own case, this is not the Defence case, but on their own case, the perpetrators could have been out. We say that is enough, in and of itself, to acquit Mr. Kubura. Even the Prosecution would also have to concede that on the face of their own indictment, there is a contradiction. Mr. Kubura is not charged for offences in Guca Gora and Travnik where the indictment alleges the Mujahedin were present. How do they make such a distinction? Also, the Prosecution didn't initially charge Mr. Kubura for the offences in Miletici. They only added that after Dusina been removed following Appeals Chamber's judgement. And although I don't want to go into the all the detail, but Your Honours will know that in the Prosecution pre-trial brief, the Prosecution set out what their evidence was for Miletici when they managed to get the charge added. That was at paragraphs 53 to 56. And having reviewed the paragraphs and that evidence again before today the evidence is simply not there. They mention a resubordination order which has nothing to do with Miletici and they mention two witnesses who talk about the 7th Brigade arriving in Miletici. But when one examines the testimony of those witnesses, they never said anything about the 7th Brigade coming to Miletici on 24 April or before. In our submission, very clear and firm links must be made between the alleged perpetrator and Mr. Kubura if the Prosecution is going to seek to prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. The Prosecution knows this and they have been attempting to make such links. I wish now to briefly mention only a few of those attempt links to show how, in our Defence case, it will be made clear that those links are not there. In truth they do not exist. Firstly there is at Turkish guerilla. This matter in our submission has been dealt with already. There is testimony that makes it quite clear that this group was not part of the 7th Brigade. No documents mention the 7th Brigade in relation to the Turkish guerilla. Our witnesses will confirm exactly that. In any event, there's no connection between the Turkish guerilla and the offences in Miletici and Maline. Secondly, the Prosecution has raised the question which Mr. Kubura asked about the Mujahedin at the meeting of the 3rd Corps on the 20th of June 1993. That was P429. It was recorded in those minutes that apparently he asked, "Will the Mujahedin continue to be engaged?" There was a translation problem but that was clarified. "Will they go to Mount Igman or will they continue to conduct combat operations in the zone of operations of the 3rd Corps?" However, in our submission, it would be reasonable to ask such a question at a meeting on the 23rd of June when General Delic's earlier order of 16 June 1993 was for the Mujahedin to be sent to Igman. That's P270. And there is testimony before Your Honours that all officers would have known about that order. In this context, the Prosecution might seek to raise document P616, another translation problem about Arabs wanting to go to Igman. But this is much later. This is 27 August 1993. The document has nothing to do with Mr. Kubura and nothing to do with Miletici or Maline. Thirdly, there's the allegation that members of the 7th Brigade were involved in a demining operation on 24 May 1993 in the Bila valley. That's Mr. Sipic's report DH1053 and a new document P951. This information, on the face of the document, originally came from the HVO, and the involvement of members of the 7th Brigade in such an operation was not confirmed in the testimony of the witnesses. In any event, how does this demining operation show that the 7th Brigade was involved in any operations in Miletici and Maline bearing in mind that all witnesses of the 306th Brigade confirmed that the 7th Brigade was not involved. Fourthly, there are the documents that purport to mention the 7th Brigade in relation to Mehurici. The Prosecution has sought to mention many of these documents. Your Honours have also raised questions about these documents, and we said we will return to our case which we will do. For instance, there's document P481, an unsigned document with no name talking about the resubordination of 20 troops from the Mehurici sector. Your Honours heard the testimony of the witness that it was not possible to resubordinate in this fashion, and Your Honours will hear further evidence about that alleged document. Then there's document P663 of 5 May 1993 which talked about the need to resolve the status of the Mujahedin and members of the 17th or 7th Muslim Brigade quartered in Mehurici. But Mr. Sipic clarified this matter in we say, in his testimony. He said he was referring to renegade individuals that had left the 7th Brigade and that their status needed to be resolved. Also, Your Honours have heard the evidence and this will be confirmed that the 1st Battalion of the 7th Brigade was in the town of Mehurici -- in the town of Travnik. That's where they were based, not in Mehurici. This will be confirmed by our witnesses and they will address other documents P471 and P474, a document which the first witness will be called will address when he gives his testimony before Your Honours. On this point, in our submission, it is significant, but in the original indictment, the one that went right back to 2001, the OTP had charged Mr. Kubura for the incidents in the Mehurici elementary school and the blacksmith shop. But when we challenged these charges on the basis that it was not alleged in the indictment that the 7th Brigade was there, being only alleged that the Mujahedin were there, the Prosecution withdrew those charges. And in the second indictment and in the third indictment, he is not charged for the incidents in the Mehurici elementary school and the blacksmith shop. That's at paragraph 20 of the original indictment. If the 7th Brigade was in Mehurici, why did the Prosecution withdraw those charges? This leads me on to the fifth attempted link and that is Mr. Ramo Durmis. In the words of Mr. Waespi he was described as a "prominent figure," but by Mr. Durmis's own account, he left the 7th Brigade April 1993, in other words before Miletici and Maline. That's document P941 a document the Prosecution has been seeking to introduce. We do not disagree with the Prosecution's own document but, moreover, our witnesses from the 7th Brigade will state that Mr. Durmis left the brigade earlier - April, 1993 - after the operations in Visoko in December 1992. The citation that has been referred to, that's P727 where Mr. Durmis's name has been mentioned will, on the testimony, be shown to relate to events in 1992, those in Visoko. The award was given to the 1st Battalion, not to Mr. Durmis himself, and it related to events in 1992. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Lastly, to the extent that the Prosecution might seek to link him with an interview conducted by Witness ZP, that's document P598, the person who was interviewed never said he was with the 7th Brigade when he participated in the kidnappings of Mr. Totic and when he was involved, as he says, in Miletici. We will also invite Your Honours to look at what Witness ZP said about the person he interviewed, that he was a complete fool and he did not take him seriously at all. The last attempted link which relates to the subject of names is that those names mentioned in the HVO document, that's P561 about the people involved in Miletici, none of them were ever members of the 7th Brigade and no other names that have been mentioned in the evidence, whether they are local or foreign were members of the 7th Brigade. In our submission, each and every attempt to make a link fails because, in truth, there is no such link. Your Honours, moving now on to the rest of the indictment against Mr. Kubura, in many ways an indictment within an indictment which does not concern the Mujahedin. Count 4, the Zenica music school. The Defence does not dispute that some beatings occurred at the music school; that has been clear from the beginning. But paragraph 41 (A) of the indictment says persons that were kept there from 1 April to at least January 1994; however, according to witness testimony, it was months earlier that people were no longer detained there and the main incidents really occurred in May and June of 1993. However, the key issue here is where is the evidence that Mr. Kubura knew or had reason to know about these particular incidents? No evidence is identified in the Prosecution pre-trial brief or the 98 bis submission other than to say that the offences were notorious and that rumours were rife. But not a single report send or received by Mr. Kubura, not a single meeting on the matter, not a single complaint made to Mr. Kubura, not a single visit, indeed, not a single reference to him in respect of the music school. Mr. Merdan and Mr. Dugalic both visited the music school and found nothing to report. As the superiors of Mr. Kubura, if they had no reason to act, how could he be expected to do more? Neither of them consults Mr. Kubura about the music school. Was this because he was not regarded as the commander at the time in charge, bearing in mind when the alleged incidents occurred. In any event, in our submission, general rumours are not enough. There must be evidence that Mr. Kubura had some information that crimes were suspected. According to the Blaskic Appeals Chamber decision, that is the standard. It is necessary for the Prosecution to introduce evidence of information being available to Mr. Kubura that would put him on notice of offences committed by persons in the music school. There's no such evidence in this case. In addition, the evidence has confirmed that if there were any reports of beatings, they would have passed through the security organs of the brigade directly to the 3rd Corps command security organs. That is the usual chain of command for security matters regarding prisoners held by the military police; in other words, not through the brigade command. Such reports may well not have been made at all. As the evidence suggests that subordinates had every motivation to hide from the command what they were up to. Beating persons for personal revenge, gratification, exchanges of family, and financial gain. Of course once the evidence emerges of suspected crimes, the command must act swiftly and decisively. Proceedings have now been brought against those responsible for the music school, including Mr. Jasmin Isic [phoen]. The Prosecution will say there has been too much of a delay but in our submission, Article 7(3) does not place a time limit on the punishment process. The perpetrators are being proceeded against. Count 4, Motel Sretno. As alleged in the indictment, the incidents there occurred over a very limited period of time from 18 May to 21 June. In other words, before 6 August 1993. The witnesses all testified that they were released within 24 hours of having been detained on 18 May 1993. There is no evidence that Mr. Kubura was ever informed about these incidents or was at the motel or in the vicinity at the material time. No evidence that he received any reports or complaints about these beatings. Once again, there can be no basis for concluding that he knew or had any reason to know about these beatings. Lastly, Counts 5 and 6, destruction and looting. This is for the Ovnak area and Vares, two operations that Mr. Kubura was involved in. Significantly, though, no evidence that Mujahedin were involved in these operations. Once again, undermining the Prosecution position that the 7th Brigade acted with the Mujahedin in spearheading crucial operations. Ovnak and Vares were one of the most significant operations conducted during that time period. If the Mujahedin were spearheading, well why isn't the evidence that they were there in those operations? Firstly, on the crime base there is no dispute and there never has been that some lootings occurred but the issue is timing. When did they occur and who were the perpetrators? In respect of the alleged destruction, in Vares, there is no evidence of such destruction. Your Honours heard about cross-firing into buildings when troops arrived, but this is a standard military procedure for first entering a defended town and can hardly be characterised as devastation of a town not justified by military necessity. Destruction must be on a large scale in order to qualify as a crime under the jurisdiction of the ICTY. For the destruction in Ovnak, the issue, again, is when and by whom? The evidence is so far that either there was no destruction observed by the Prosecution witnesses in June 1993, or that the damage was caused by legitimate military action, and there is evidence that destruction took place after June 1993. The operations involved many brigades, many units, and civilians were also present at the time. Mr. Kubura can only be held responsible for the acts of his subordinates and not those of the members of other brigades or units or civilians. In respect of the lootings, our witnesses will confirm that the 7th Brigade withdrew on each occasion, as a manoeuvre unit does, immediately after the military operations concluded and before any looting commenced. The only evidence that could be used against the 7th Brigade is in respect of Vares where, to the extent that anyone was recognised as a member of the brigade, they were seen taking bread, and on one occasion, women's shoes. These are minor matters, Your Honour, which simply do not rise to the level of seriousness required by this Tribunal. Likewise in Ovnak, no evidence that the 7th Brigade committed these offences. Many brigades were present, police forces, and civilians who observed looting as well, and evidence that looting occurred after June 1993, the time period in the indictment. Turning to my concluding remarks, Your Honour, the cornerstone of the Tribunal's procedure, irrespective of what national jurisdiction we come from, is that the Prosecution bear the burden of proving the case. That is provided for in Rule 87. The standard is beyond reasonable doubt. Anything less obliges the triers of fact to acquit and the accused is always entitled to the benefit of the doubt as to whether the offence has been proved or not. This has been applied in many judgements. The bottom line for us is that the Prosecution have not proved their case beyond a reasonable doubt, and where there is doubt, the Chamber must acquit. It might seem trite but it is a fundamental obligation in a system of international justice, and one by which the ICTY itself will be judged by history. It is a principle that was that was strongly underlined by the Celebici Trial Chamber in its judgement which is probably one of the most referred to judgements on the doctrine of command responsibility and I quote from paragraph 377 of that judgement where the Trial Chamber said, "The doctrine of command responsibility is ultimately predicated upon the power of the superior to control the acts of his subordinates. Great care must be taken lest an injustice be committed in holding individuals responsible for the acts of others in situations where the link of control is absent or too remote." Your Honours, Mr. Kubura will not testify in his case. He's not obliged to and that cannot be held against him. There is no need to, as there is no evidence beyond a reasonable doubt that links him to any of the alleged offences. He has barely even been mentioned throughout this entire trial. Some witnesses will be called merely to confirm that the 7th Brigade had nothing to do with the alleged killings and the other offences. We will start with Travnik, covering the alleged killings in Miletici and Maline, and then we will move on to the rest of the indictment. We will not lead evidence in relation to the context or in relation to the activities of other brigades or of the 3rd Corps and its command. Our focus will be on the 7th Brigade and the allegations that are made against it in the indictment. At the outset, as I have said, Mr. Kubura will provide a brief statement to Your Honours in terms of Rule 84 bis, with Your Honours to determine the probative value to be given to such a statement. He simply wishes to make his position quite clear that he had nothing to do with these alleged crimes. I conclude with returning to the Prosecutor's indictment and the fundamental allegation which is set out in paragraph 38. "At all times relevant to this indictment, Amir Kubura exercised effective control over all his subordinates alleged to have committed crimes." But which subordinates exactly of Mr. Kubura do the Prosecution say and show in the evidence committed the alleged killings and offences? All four indictments are silent on that matter. The evidence is silent, and the Prosecution is still silent. As Your Honours have remarked on many occasions, this is an adversarial truth-seeking exercise. Have the Prosecution taken us closer to the truth in the presentation and examination of the evidence? Yes, they have, in fact, on the actual evidence. Leaving aside the comments and the oversimplifications that they've made, the evidence shows that Mr. Kubura did not effectively control any Mujahedin perpetrators, and he's not criminally responsible for any of the offences charged. Our Defence case will confirm that and we respectively ask Your Honours to confirm that in your judgement. Thank you, Your Honours. With your leave, I would now request that Mr. Kubura be given an opportunity to make his statement and thereafter, we will call the first witness in his Defence case. I'm grateful for this opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Dixon. Mr. Kubura, you may stand and pursuant to Rule 84 bis (A) you may make a statement. I give you the floor now. THE ACCUSED KUBURA: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honours, I will focus on the following. First, my biography and my background up until the time the indictment was brought. Secondly, my engagement in the course of the war, and I will focus on the time spent in the 7th Muslim brigade. I will then deal or, rather, address the allegations in the indictment. I was born on the 4th of March 1964 in Kakanj in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Having completed primary school, I completed the secondary military school in Mostar and then the academy for ground forces in Belgrade. In 1987, I graduated from the academy and I was promoted to the rank of second lieutenant. I was then sent or, rather, appointed to the duty of a commander of the platoon in Djakovici in Kosovo. After a year in the military service, I was promoted to the rank of lieutenant. Three years later I was appointed as commander of a border company. In the first half of 1991 in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, the military and political situation deteriorated and the situation came to a climax when the former Yugoslavia broke down and Slovenia declared its independence, which the then-JNA attempted to prevent by using force. And as a result, the first victims fell. Officers and soldiers in Slovenia, Slovenian officers and soldiers left the JNA and he we drew from Slovenia. In the second half of 1991, the military situation was transferred to Croatia and this caused Croatian officers and soldiers to leave the JNA. At the end of 1991 and at the beginning of 1992, Macedonians and Bosniaks also started leaving the JNA, and it became evident that the rump Yugoslav Peoples' Army had become an army composed of one ethnic group, composed of only Serbian and Montenegrin soldiers and officers. At the beginning of 1992 I sent a request to my command in Djakovici in which I requested that I leave the JNA because I couldn't see a role for me in that army since it was conducting a war against my people or, rather, against its own people. At the beginning of April 1992, since they did not want to let me leave the JNA, I decided to leave of my own accord and to leave Kosovo and go to Bosnia and Herzegovina, to my birthplace, which is where my parents, family and friends lived. I left together with my wife and my two children, one of which was 16-months old and the other 3-months old. I left Kosovo and I went to Macedonia. Given the war that was raging in Croatia, and had only just broken out in Bosnia and Herzegovina, I had to leave with my family via Macedonia. I first went from Macedonia to Bulgaria, then to Romania, then to Hungary, then to Croatia, and only then to Bosnia and Herzegovina. I had no contact with my parents and relatives for over a month as they didn't know where we were nor what had happened to us. They didn't know whether we were alive. At the beginning of 1992, I went to Kakanj to stay with family members and as of that date I was engaged in the Kakanj Municipality Defence Staff by order of the command of the 3rd Corps. Dated the 11th of December 1992. I was appointed as the assistant chief of staff for operations in training in the 7th Muslim Brigade Staff, and at the first meeting -- in the 7th Muslim Brigade, I was called to the first meeting in the 7th Muslim Brigade by the they be command of the 7th Muslim Brigade Karajilic Mahmut [phoen]. This was on the 24th of December 1992. That's the first time I came to know the command -- the commander of the brigade and the chief of staff of the 7th Muslim Brigade Asim Koricic, who was my immediate superior in the Brigade. They gave me the duty to transfer my duty of the demander of the battalion which I had performed up until that time to my deputy Osman Ibrahim Spahic and by mid-January 1993 I was to report to the 7th Muslim Brigade to take over my duties. By order of the Supreme Command staff dated the 12th of March, 1993, I was appointed as the chief of staff of the 7th Muslim Brigade and the chief of staff of the 7th Muslim Brigade, the person who had been the chief of staff of the 7th Muslim Brigade up until that time, Asim Koricic, was appointed to the position of the brigade commander by order of the Supreme Command Staff dated 6th of August, 1993. I was appointed as the commander of the 7th Muslim Brigade and also an appointment was made ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, please speak a little more slowly because the interpreters are finding it difficult to follow you. THE ACCUSED KUBURA: [Interpretation] By an order of the president dated the 16th of March 1994, I was transferred to the Sarajevo 1st Corps as commander of the brigade. And towards 1995, at the end of 1995, I was transferred to the post of commander of the brigade in Konjic. It was the end of 1997, I was appointed as the deputy commander of the division in Sarajevo. At the end of the war, when the Dayton agreement had been signed, in -- and the troops were demobilised, and a professional army was formed, which was created in accordance with the NATO standards and in accordance with the programme "equip and train." The plan equip and train was a plan that NATO officers were in charge of, mainly American officers, and a selection was made of officers who were to be trained and who attended a course. After this selection had been made, I was sent to attend a course in a school for foreign languages. I was sent to attend the Staff Officer's College, a course for commanding a brigade, a course for commanding the corps staff, and, of course, for carrying out combat operations in a simulation centre. All of this in accordance with NATO standards. At the end of 1999 and the beginning of 2000, in the federation army, the Bosniak part received the task of performing 5 professional brigades and one brigade in Sarajevo, one in Tuzla, one in Mostar, one in Bihac, and one in Gorazde. It was necessary to select five brigade commanders when selecting these officers. I was selected as the commander of a professional brigade located in Sarajevo, and on that occasion I was promoted to the rank of brigadier. At the beginning of 2001, when an indictment was brought against me, I was with my wife and three children in Croatia at the sea. In 1996, I had a third child. I was informed over the phone about the indictment, and without giving it any thought, I returned to Sarajevo and reported to the Bosnia and Herzegovinian authorities and placed myself at the disposal of the Tribunal. I signed a document saying that I would voluntarily surrender to The Hague and as of the 4th of August 2001, I have been in the Detention Unit in Scheveningen. Why have I come here? For two reasons: Firstly, because I knew and felt that I was not guilty and that the allegations in the indictment with which I have been charged are erroneous. Secondly, I have absolutely no doubts and I have full confidence in this International Tribunal and in this Trial Chamber, which I believe will realise that the events of which I have been charged with have nothing to do with me. I will support this claim by referring to some facts that have recently been discussed and that will be discussed in the course of my Defence. Your Honours, I will now address the period relevant to the charges levelled against me and I will address the counts in the indictment. When I first saw the indictment and read through it, when I read through the charges that concerned Maline and Miletici, I asked my counsel to tell me where these villages were located and asked him to bring me a map. I asked him to do this because I had never heard where -- about the of Miletici and Maline. I didn't know where they were and the first time I became aware of their existence was when I read the indictment. Your Honours, in the course of this trial and the proceedings that commenced in December of 2003, you have had the occasion to listen to the testimony of many witnesses and to examine numerous documents. I was certain then and I'm certain now that while I was in the 7th Muslim Brigade, my soldiers and I were never involved in combat activity of any kind in those villages. It's obvious that these events did take place in Miletici and Maline on the 24th of April and the 8th of June 1993; however, it is also obvious that the 7th Muslim Brigade are -- not a single part of the 7th Muslim Brigade had a task to perform there, nor did the 7th Muslim Brigade participate in combat of any kind in those villages. It is also correct to say that the Prosecution and Defence witnesses have testified here, and at in point in time did they mention that the 7th Muslim Brigade participated in the events in those villages; on the contrary, they claimed that the 7th Muslim Brigade was not there and was not involved in combat activity. It is quite obvious that witnesses, officers, and soldiers have confirmed this, individuals who weren't members of the 7th Muslim Brigade but they were from the Bosanska Krajina Operative Group from the 306th, the 314th, and the 312th Brigade. And the villages of Miletici and Maline were located in those zones of responsibility, and they quite clearly stated who was responsible for those events. The superior command did not request the 7th Muslim Brigade to submit reports of any kind about the events in Miletici and Maline. In the HVO reports and ABiH reports, no one mentions the participation of the 7th Muslim Brigade in those events, not in any respect. This is quite understandable. It wasn't possible to ask the 7th Muslim Brigade to submit a report since the 7th Muslim Brigade did not participate in the events. In the course of the proceedings, it has been established that Mujahedin were responsible for what happened in the villages of Miletici and Maline, and no one established a connection between the 7th Muslim Brigade and these events. In the course of these proceedings, it has been established that these individuals were not members of the 7th Muslim Brigade, and it has been established that I had no control over the Mujahedin. No one invited 7th Muslim Brigade officers or myself to negotiate or to discussions concerning a problem of the Mujahedin. No one asked for a report about the Mujahedin. Your Honours, you have heard the testimony of witnesses according to which there were problems that they had caused and you have heard the testimony of witnesses who asked to come and discuss matters with them. But no one ever asked me to become involved in negotiations or discussions with them, and no one ever provided me with any reports or any information about them. It's quite understandable that there is no such correspondence because I can't be responsible for the acts of individuals who were not members of my unit. The music school and Sretno hotel. Your Honours, in the course of the trial I found out -- became aware that certain events happened at the school. I found out about that in the course of testimony of people who for brief periods of time spent time there. But in the same way when I was a member of the 7th Muslim Brigade, have never known anything or received any information as to what was taking place at music school and Sretno motel. Everything I knew was that music school was a detention centre and that it was the headquarters of the military police and that the 3rd Battalion was stationed at Motel Sretno. I have never visited or spent time at the music school and all tasks and duties with respect to music school were carried out by the security services. The Trial so far, the proceedings so far, have indicated that no witness or no piece of evidence ever established a link between myself and the events at music school and Motel Sretno. Not a single witness had ever heard of me or of ever seen me or mentioned me in their testimony. Witnesses who testified and visited and carried out controls of music school premises, either announced or unannounced, had never contacted me either prior to or after those controls and never mentioned me in any other context. It is also the case with regard to the representatives of the international organisations, institutions which were present in Zenica and visited music school at that time. Had I known anything at all about the irregularities and abuse there, it is quite certain that within my power, I would have introduced the measures and taken steps to make sure that such things did not happen again, and to punish the perpetrators in the same way in which I did in all the other cases in the course of my duties. The same applies to Motel Sretno because at that period of time, I was involved in combat operations 20 kilometres away from Kakanj. In this case, too, there's no document, no witness making a reference to me and I was in no way informed or aware of those events. Susanj, Ovnak, Brajkovici, and Grahovcici. As to the events at the beginning of June 1993 in the area of Ovnak, it is correct that the 2nd and the 3rd Battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade did participate within the framework of the tactics group which was set up on the basis of superior command orders with regard to combat activities. The 7th Muslim Brigade did participate in those combat activities, together with the units of the 314th Brigade, the Anti-sabotage Unit of the Municipal Staff Zenica and the Manevar unit. The tactic group carried out this task on the 9th of June 1993 and already on the 10th and the 11th of June 1993, the 7th Muslim Brigade left the area and went to the area of Kakanj when the -- where the HVO offensive had already started. This indicates, in much the same way as the other facts which have been established, that the members of the 7th Muslim Brigade did not participate in looting and the destruction of property in this area, also because very soon after the end of the operation, we left the area. So de facto, the 7th Muslim Brigade would have been unable to do that anyway. In the same way, Your Honours, if you can just think back of the statements made by some witnesses who asked to visit the area of Ovnak, you will see that they never asked for such authorisation from the 7th Muslim Brigade, that is to say, after the 10th of June, because that Brigade was not stationed in the area. We've heard some witnesses talk about other units having been set up and then they came and were in charge of the security situation in the area. But there was no mention of the 7th Muslim Brigade Vares. The 7th Muslim Brigade on the basis of the order of the Superior Command was supposed to take part in the liberation of Vares. In those combat activities, we had units of the 2nd the 3rd Corps and the 6th Corps. It is undisputable that the units of the 2nd the 3rd and 6th Corps enter the city of the Vares on the 4th of November 1993, and it is also obvious that the members of the 7th Muslim Brigade entered the city of Vares without any combat activity taking place. The city had already been partially looted and set on fire on the part of the members of the HVO and they -- who had left. I, myself, who at the time was a commander of the 7th Muslim Brigade on the 5th of November 1993 ordered the withdrawal of my own units from Vares, and that order was obeyed. And on the 6th of November, the unit left Vares and went back to Zenica. In the same way, I ordered for checkpoints to be set up for control purposes within the framework of an effort, an overall effort aimed at preventing any illegal activities. The destruction and the looting did not take place at Vares and especially not on the part of the members of the 7th Muslim Brigade which left Vares as early as the 6th of November 1993. Amongst other things, we've heard earlier on that witnesses saw one soldier coming out with a pair of shoes out of a shoe shop and somebody else was carrying bread and chocolates and a witness mentioned that a group of people had been chased away from a flower warehouse by UN members and they were unable to take anything, and so on and so forth. Your Honours, before I conclude, I'd just like to point out a number of facts which have to do with my duties, my establishment duties. On the 12th of March, I was made the chief of staff and on the 6th of August, the Brigade Commander. Up to that point, I had never received any orders about representing the commander in his absence or any orders to take over the duty aimed at a final solution or until such time as the commander was able to come back. Since I was surprised by the situation, I was basically forced to somehow continue as I was awaiting an order or an appointment of somebody else to this position of commander or awaiting some other order which would refer to myself. Since I had no formal order at that time, I, myself, as the chief of staff of the 7th Muslim Brigade, according to the indictment, was at the same time the deputy commander and the acting commander. It is obvious that this would run counter to all the rules and it is obvious that I was simply unable to carry out three different duties within the same unit. Something else that was indicated in the indictment was the date of the 1st of April which apparently indicated the date as of when I started acting as a commander. But it was a haphazardly chosen date. Your Honours, when, on the 6th of August, 1993, I was made the commander of this brigade, Mr. Halil Brzina was appointed as my deputy and Mr. Serif Patkovic was made the chief of staff. So we have three people who, on the basis of the same order, were appointed to three different jobs, which indicates that I could not at the same time be the chief of staff, the Deputy Commander, and the Acting Commander. So this is legally speaking and practically speaking impossible. Now I come to my conclusion. Your Honours, on the basis of the proceedings so far, the facts have indicated the following: One, that the that the 7th Muslim Brigade did not participate in the events that took place at the villages of Miletici and Maline. Two, that I did not know and that I was in no way informed or familiar with the events at music school and Motel Sretno. Three, that the 7th Muslim Brigade did not participate in the destruction and the looting of the following villages: Susanj, Ovnak, Brajkovici, and Grahovcici, and the city of Vares. And four, the counts in the indictment accusing me of these facts have not been proven with regard to myself. Your Honours, I reported to this court voluntarily in order to prove my innocence on the counts of the indictment. When there was a meeting with regard to the request for temporary release in December of 2001, Judge Schaumburg pointed out to my behaviour and my attitude to the Tribunal, and set it up as an example. He asked for my officer's word to prove that I would come back at the time of the start of the trial. I have come back and now I'm giving you my officer's and my word, and my word as a man, that I'm not guilty. Let justice prevail. Your Honours, thank you for your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, then. You may sit down, General. You have just made your statement in line with the provisions of our Statute. It is now 5.25 so it is a good time to have a break now and at the end of the break, we shall hear the witness and then we'll continue until 7.00. So we'll start again at ten to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we can continue and I'd like to ask the usher to bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. Let me first of all check that you can hear the translation of what I'm saying in your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, we've asked you to come in somewhat late because we were busy working on other points that we had to deal with prior to your arrival, so we do apologise for the fact that you've had to wait. Now, we shall first of all listen to your oath -- first of all, however, I need you to give me your name and family name and the place and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Semir Terzic, I was born on the 30th of November, 1957.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell us whether you have a profession or a job at the moment, and if so, which one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I work at the defence unit of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have a rank, are you an officer or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am a professor philosophy and sociology by profession, and I'm a reserve captain. That's how I left the war, a reserve major, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Between 1992 and 1993, at that time, did you have a rank or -- a military job. If so, which one, and where were you? Where were you stationed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992, I was a professor at the grammar school and the nurses school, and that was at the beginning of the war. And then joined the army and since I was a reserve officer and I had gone to the reserve officer's course at Bilici - I was a reserve captain or a reserve senior official from the former JNA in the reserve forces of the former JNA - I joined the BH army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you joined the BH army in what specific unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since the beginning of the war, the start of the war had been declared and the municipal staff, we had a detachment that we had set up, the Muslim forces detachment at Travnik. That was on the 10th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And thereafter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the BH army brigades were set up, the 17th, somewhere mid-November, the 7th Muslim Brigade. And on the 14th of February, the 27th Light Muslim Brigade, the liberating brigade was set up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you already testified before this Court or a national court, maybe, with regard to the facts that -- and the events that happened in your country between 1993 and 1994 or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm here for the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like you to read the oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly swear that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may sit now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
